_comment: Benign traffic set (Stage 5.2, decision D1 layer 1). Normal requests to the SAME endpoints Red attacks, sent through the same HTTP client as Red, interleaved by a seeded schedule that preserves this list's order. Every entry is genuinely benign by the SENDER'S INTENT (contract 10). Designer-approved 2026-11-09. Verified empirically (tools/verify_benign_set.py): expected_solves lists the challenges an entry is known to solve; only challenges NOT in config/challenge_map.json are allowed there, and the benign_solved_challenge tripwire fires when the observed newly_solved set differs from it in any way. `requires` names an earlier entry this one depends on (sent after it, verified together). Never tune this set or Blue's signatures against each other.

entries.note: An unregistered visitor tries to log in (expect 401).
A real user mistypes their password (expect 401).
Empty search: what the shop's own front page sends.
A public file in the FTP folder.
A customer tracks an order (Juice Shop's order-id format).
A new customer registers (the shop's registration endpoint). Precedes n11.
The customer registered in n10 logs in successfully (expect 200), so 'login 200' is not a shortcut for 'attack'.
SQL keyword UNION as an ordinary word.
SQL keyword DROP as a candy name.
An angle bracket from a heart emoticon (looks like XSS).
A quote and '--' in a PASSWORD. The password is hashed before the query (Red's negative control shows the field is not injectable), so no SQL is touched (expect 401).
An XSS keyword as a search term.

A person named O'Brien logs in (contract 10). Benign by intent; the apostrophe breaks Juice Shop's injectable login query, so the server answers 500 and solves 'Error Handling' (its bug, not an attack). The textbook false positive for naive SQLi signatures.
